dedupe_keys.name: united states surgical quality and access after rural hospital closures 2010 to 2020

description: This case study evaluates whether rural hospital closures changed the quality of and access to common surgery. The authors, researchers at the University of Michigan, the University of South Carolina and the University of Chicago, used Medicare claims from 2010 to 2020 and a dynamic difference-in-differences design for colectomy, cholecystectomy, appendectomy and hernia repair, and published the work in an open-access journal article. The analysis covers 36,884 beneficiaries who lost their nearest rural hospital and 41,185 who lost their second-nearest. Coverage is rural areas across the United States. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence; the claims data need a data use agreement. Caveats: only fee-for-service Medicare patients and four operations are included, and travel distance is a proxy for access. The study found no significant change in 30-day mortality, complications, serious complications, reoperations or readmissions, and no change in rates of unplanned surgery; however, median travel distance rose from 13.1 to 16.4 miles for patients who lost their nearest hospital, and did not change for those who lost their second-nearest. Simulation uses: travel distance and outcome effects of facility closure for healthcare access and network models. Related records: the study of closures and acute and post-acute care (case_study-us-rural-hospital-closures-acute-post-acute-care) covers wider hospital use.
